architectural_implications.after: Trace capture plus attached user feedback is the upstream supply of the offline eval corpus that gates deployment.
architectural_implications.before: Tracing is a debugging/logging layer used reactively when something breaks.
architectural_implications.consequence: Sampling policy, feedback attachment, and dataset derivation from traces become first-class architecture decisions; gaps in tracing directly degrade improvement capability.
architectural_implications.observation: Traces become the raw material for evaluation datasets rather than a debugging afterthought.

architectural_implications.after: Agents propose prompt and code fixes; humans own and review the eval criteria and dataset scope those fixes must pass.
architectural_implications.before: Engineers hand-write prompts, criteria, and test cases in one manual pass.
architectural_implications.consequence: Eval definitions must be stored as reviewable, version-controlled artifacts inside the agent stack, and the deployment gate must be the eval result, not the author's intent.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluation criteria and dataset boundaries are held by humans while fixes are generated by agents.

architectural_implications.after: Changes at the agent-configuration level, goal-definition level, and per-turn level are tracked and gated separately.
architectural_implications.before: A single undifferentiated dev cycle: change prompt, ship, observe, repeat.
architectural_implications.consequence: Monitoring and ownership must be assigned per loop level; a regression in agent quality may originate in the goal loop, so diagnosis requires per-level telemetry, not just end-to-end metrics.
architectural_implications.observation: Improvement is organized into a meta loop, goal loop, and token loop instead of one iteration cycle.

architectural_implications.after: Agents draft changes and submit them for review, backed by explicit evaluation criteria.
architectural_implications.before: Automated output is committed directly or is entirely human-authored.
architectural_implications.consequence: The loop's throughput ceiling becomes human review capacity, so reducing review load per change (better diffs, evidence packaging) becomes the optimization target.
architectural_implications.observation: Agent-produced changes are routed through review gates rather than applied directly.

article_ideas.angle: Argue against the intuitive build order (automate the fixer first) using the observation that generation automation without specification automation just moves the queue, and pair it with the concrete contamination symptom of internal jargon reaching end users.

article_ideas.thesis: The dominant failure of automated agent improvement is not bad fix generation but a misaligned eval substrate: because targets shift and curation is manual, the loop converges confidently on stale criteria, so the correct investment order is dataset lifecycle and criteria versioning before fix automation.

core_insights.generalization: Any adaptive system needs separated control planes for 'execute', 'define success', and 'change the executor'; mixing them collapses into reward hacking or unguided drift.
core_insights.insight: Self-improving agent stacks are structured as a hierarchy of loops with distinct scopes and cadences — a roadmap/meta loop, a goal loop, and an agent-turn/token loop — where improvement work happens at a different level than task execution.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete decomposition for where improvement logic lives: the inner token loop optimizes a single run, the goal loop defines what the run should achieve, and the meta loop changes the agent itself. Engineers must decide which artifacts (prompts, tools, eval criteria, datasets) each loop is permitted to mutate, because conflating them lets the agent rewrite its own success criteria.

evidence_quotes.text: Design agent workflows to be read-intensive rather than write-intensive by letting agents analyze traces.
I don't write prompts anymore. I have loops.

Early agent systems required heavy manual prompt writing and debugging. Modern stacks allow agents to read through vast production traces, user feedback, and evaluation results to propose improvements.

core_insights.generalization: When a system's improvement bottleneck shifts from human expression to machine observation, the winning infrastructure is the observability substrate, not the authoring surface.
core_insights.insight: The agent workflow inverts from write-intensive (humans authoring and debugging prompts) to read-intensive (agents ingesting large volumes of production traces, user feedback, and eval results and proposing the changes).
core_insights.why_it_matters: This changes the primary engineering input from human authoring effort to data availability and trace quality. It implies the highest-leverage investment is making execution data machine-readable and complete, not writing better prompts by hand. It also shifts the cost model toward large-context reading of traces.

evidence_quotes.text: Manual labor is currently bottlenecking the loop when updating datasets, evaluation criteria, and proposing fixes.

core_insights.generalization: Automation applied to the fast part of a pipeline (generation) without automating the slow part (specification/verification) just moves the queue.
core_insights.insight: The binding constraint in the improvement loop is not fix generation but manual maintenance of datasets and evaluation criteria; automated fix proposals are only as useful as the continuously curated eval substrate underneath them.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Teams that automate prompt/code fixes without automating or resourcing dataset curation get fast iteration against stale or wrong criteria. It reorders priorities: dataset lifecycle and criteria ownership are the real engineering surface, and any 'self-improving' stack must budget for the eval side of the loop.

evidence_quotes.text: Humans should remain involved in setting evaluation criteria, maintaining datasets, and reviewing proposed fixes to prevent over-fitting and prompt sloppy agent behavior.

core_insights.generalization: In self-modifying systems, the agent must never own the oracle. Delegate generation, retain specification and boundary-setting.
core_insights.insight: Human-in-the-loop placement should not be uniform: humans retain ownership of evaluation criteria and dataset boundaries, while agents are delegated fix proposal and criteria maintenance within those boundaries.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is a specific allocation rule rather than generic 'keep a human in the loop'. Granting the agent write access to its own evaluators is the failure path; granting it write access to the code/prompt fix while the human owns the grader keeps the loop corrigible. It defines an enforceable interface for the meta loop.

evidence_quotes.text: If agents completely automate the creation of evaluation datasets and fixes without human oversight, they risk overfitting to quirks and introducing jargon leakage.
Customer support agents leaking internal pipeline jargon to end users.

core_insights.generalization: Any pipeline that converts production logs into improvement signal inherits the logs' incidental context; contamination becomes regressions in the output distribution, not just noise in metrics.
core_insights.insight: Fully automated dataset/fix generation produces a concrete, observable failure mode: overfitting to trace quirks and leaking internal pipeline jargon into user-facing output.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is a checkable symptom rather than an abstract risk — internal vocabulary appearing in customer-facing text is a detectable signal that the agent learned from traces including internal context rather than from task-relevant behavior. It implies trace data carries context contamination that must be filtered before becoming training/eval material.

evidence_quotes.text: Targets for AI agents are inherently incomplete and shift constantly.

core_insights.generalization: For underspecified objectives, the measuring instrument needs its own update loop and change history, or it becomes the dominant hidden bug.
core_insights.insight: Agent targets are inherently incomplete and shift over time, which makes evaluation criteria themselves a live, versioned artifact rather than a fixed benchmark.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If specs are unstable, a static eval suite silently becomes misaligned with the current goal, so the loop optimizes toward yesterday's objective. Architecturally, eval criteria must live in the same versioned, reviewable change pipeline as the agent configuration they gate.

evidence_quotes.text: Production traces and user feedback are captured online, fed into offline evaluation datasets, tested against new candidate prompts or agent configurations, and redeployed after verification.
Bridging online observability with offline experimentation is critical for moving beyond manual agent maintenance.

core_insights.generalization: In adaptive systems, telemetry is a production input to the model/tool improvement process, so its completeness and schema stability are correctness concerns.
core_insights.insight: Production tracing data and offline evaluation are the same continuous artifact pipeline: online traces plus user feedback become offline datasets, which gate candidate prompt/agent configurations before redeployment.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Observability stops being a debugging utility and becomes the eval supply chain. This dictates that trace capture, feedback attachment, and dataset derivation be designed as one system with quality guarantees, not bolted on after launch.

deep_dives.why: If targets are inherently incomplete and shifting, a static eval suite silently optimizes toward yesterday's objective. Cadence is the cheapest lever on that mismatch, and the review gate makes throughput a human-capacity constraint, so the sweep has a real cost axis on both sides.

deep_dives.why: Routing agent changes through review gates makes human review the bottleneck of an otherwise automated loop. project_ideas.hypothesis: A fully automated trace-to-dataset curation loop produces measurably more internal-vocabulary leakage in user-facing output than a human-gated loop, and a leaked-vocabulary detector computed over internal-only trace fields catches these regressions before semantic eval scores do.
project_ideas.measurement: Leakage rate per 1,000 user-facing outputs in automated vs gated arms; fraction of leaks flagged by the detector before any semantic eval delta appears; false-positive rate on clean outputs.
project_ideas.name: Leak Gate
project_ideas.poc: Instrument a customer-support agent's traces with a marker set of internal-only field values (pipeline names, tool identifiers, internal status strings). Derive eval datasets two ways (automated vs human-approved boundaries), run the same candidate fixes through both, and run the leak detector as a mandatory deployment gate. Report leakage rate and lead time between leak detection and score-based detection.

project_ideas.based_on: Which loop level should absorb a given production failure, and how is that attributed?
project_ideas.hypothesis: Production agent failures can be classified into token-loop, goal-loop, and meta-loop origin from trace features with materially better than chance accuracy, and routing fixes by predicted loop level reduces iteration count to resolution versus unconditional prompt-level fixing.
project_ideas.measurement: Classifier accuracy and confusion between goal-loop and meta-loop defects; mean iterations to eval-set pass; rate of churn where a correct fix is applied at the wrong level and reverted.
project_ideas.name: Loop-Level Fault Router
project_ideas.poc: Take a seeded set of injected defects at each loop level (bad tool call formatting; contradictory goal spec; agent-config regression) on a single agent, capture traces, label by loop level, and train a lightweight classifier. Then run two fix pipelines: always-attempt-prompt-fix vs route-by-classifier, and count iterations to green.

project_ideas.based_on: What is the optimal frequency for running agent self-improvement loops in production?
project_ideas.hypothesis: Beyond some threshold, increasing meta-loop cadence stops improving eval scores and instead increases regression rate, because criteria updates lag target drift and the review queue saturates.
project_ideas.measurement: Eval score versus cadence curve with saturation point; regressions per accepted change; review minutes per accepted change; correlation between criteria staleness and production failure modes.
project_ideas.name: Cadence Sweep
project_ideas.poc: Run the same trace corpus and fix-proposal agent on per-merge, daily, and weekly cadences against a deliberately drifting objective. Track eval score, out-of-distribution regression count, eval-set staleness (age of criteria vs. observed failure modes), and human review minutes per accepted change.

project_ideas.hypothesis: Agent-proposed changes bundled with the failing trace, the eval delta, and an estimated blast radius are accepted at equal quality but in significantly less reviewer time than raw prompt diffs, which raises the loop's effective throughput ceiling.
project_ideas.measurement: Median review seconds per change; acceptance rate and post-merge revert rate as quality controls; variance in review time across reviewers as a proxy for review confidence.
project_ideas.name: Evidence-Packaged Change Review
project_ideas.poc: Build a reviewer-facing diff format that auto-attaches the triggering trace, before/after eval results on the gated dataset, and the set of affected test cases. Run a within-subject comparison where engineers review the same batch of agent-proposed fixes in raw-diff and evidence-packaged form.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Marc Klingen
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Building self-improving open-source AI agent stacks with continuous feedback loops
  • Purpose: To educate AI engineers on how to build self-improving agent stacks by combining online observation with offline dataset curation, evaluation, and automated fix proposals. Marc Klingen, co-founder of Langfuse, discusses the evolution of open-source AI agent stacks and how teams are moving toward self-improving agents. By combining online tracing and monitoring with offline evaluation, dataset generation, and prompt/agent fixes, developers can create continuous improvement loops that reduce manual overhead and improve agent performance.

Topic Map

Introduction and Evolution of Agentic Workflows

  • Explanation: Marc introduces Langfuse and discusses how the AI engineering community has progressed from simple prompt-writing to building autonomous loops and research agents.
  • Key claims:
    • Models have expanded in capabilities, enabling higher-level agent loops like autosearch and autonomous debugging.
    • Building agents is different from traditional software applications, requiring a combination of online monitoring and offline evaluation.
  • Examples:
    • GitHub Copilot PR automation
    • Karpathy's autoresearch
  • Terminology:
    • OSS agent stack
    • autonomous loops
    • autosearch
  • Why it matters: Understanding the evolution of agent stacks helps engineers design systems that can leverage increasingly capable foundational models.

The Reference Process for AI Agents

  • Explanation: Outlining the lifecycle of agent development: Trace, Monitor, Build datasets, Experiment, Evaluate, and Re-deploy.
  • Key claims:
    • A robust agent stack requires bridging online production usage with offline development and benchmarking.
    • Manual labor is currently bottlenecking the loop when updating datasets, evaluation criteria, and proposing fixes.
  • Examples:
    • Tracing customer support agent runs
    • Building offline evaluation datasets from production traces
  • Terminology:
    • Trace
    • Monitor
    • Build datasets
    • Experiment
    • Evaluate
    • Replay
  • Why it matters: Bridging online observability with offline experimentation is critical for moving beyond manual agent maintenance.

Automating Agent Improvement and Human-Agent Collaboration

  • Explanation: Exploring the sweet spot of human-agent collaboration where AI proposes fixes and maintains evaluation criteria while humans set the high-level goals and boundaries.
  • Key claims:
    • Targets for AI agents are inherently incomplete and shift constantly.
    • Humans should remain involved in setting evaluation criteria, maintaining datasets, and reviewing proposed fixes to prevent over-fitting and prompt sloppy agent behavior.
    • Automating the loop reduces time investment while increasing agent quality.
  • Examples:
    • Changelog writer agent that proposes documentation updates based on merged PRs and gets reviewed by engineers.
  • Terminology:
    • meta loop
    • goal loop
    • token loop
    • evaluators
    • dataset curation
  • Why it matters: Proper human-in-the-loop placement prevents hallucination and prompt degradation while cutting down tedious engineering overhead.

Key Points

Shift from Write-Intensive to Read-Intensive Agent Workflows

  • Explanation: Early agent systems required heavy manual prompt writing and debugging. Modern stacks allow agents to read through vast production traces, user feedback, and evaluation results to propose improvements.
  • Evidence: Production tracing data combined with offline evaluation metrics.
  • Practical implication: Teams can scale agent performance without exponentially increasing human engineering hours.

The Danger of Overfitting in Autonomous Loops

  • Explanation: If agents completely automate the creation of evaluation datasets and fixes without human oversight, they risk overfitting to quirks and introducing jargon leakage.
  • Evidence: Customer support agents leaking internal pipeline jargon to end users.
  • Practical implication: Maintain human-in-the-loop review for dataset boundaries and evaluation criteria.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Continuous OSS Agent Improvement Loop

  • How it works: Production traces and user feedback are captured online, fed into offline evaluation datasets, tested against new candidate prompts or agent configurations, and redeployed after verification.
  • Components:
    • Roadmap / Meta loop
    • Goal loop
    • Agent turn / Token loop
    • Trace & Monitoring
    • Dataset curation
    • Offline Evaluation
  • When to use: When developing production-grade AI agents that need to adapt and improve based on real-world usage.

Examples & Case Studies

A changelog writer agent analyzes merged PRs, drafts changelog updates, and submits them for human or automated code review.

  • Illustrates: How an agent stack can automate developer workflows while maintaining quality through review gates.
  • Lesson: Agents can handle tedious documentation and changelog generation if backed by robust evaluation criteria and human review.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Implement robust tracing and monitoring for all agent runs.
    • Capture user feedback and failure patterns directly into offline evaluation datasets.
  • Strategic:
    • Design agent workflows to be read-intensive rather than write-intensive by letting agents analyze traces.
    • Strike the right balance of human-agent collaboration by retaining human control over eval criteria and dataset boundaries.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How can we further automate dataset curation without risking data drift or overfitting?
    • What is the optimal frequency for running agent self-improvement loops in production?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Models have matured enough to automate prompt and agent code fixes based on offline evaluation results. (technical trend)

Notable Quotes

"I don't write prompts anymore. I have loops."

Compressed Summary

  • Open-source agent stacks are evolving toward self-improvement via continuous feedback loops.
  • Combining online tracing with offline evaluation allows agents to propose prompt and code fixes.
  • Human-in-the-loop oversight is essential for setting evaluation criteria and preventing overfitting or jargon leakage.
  • Keywords: agents, observability, evaluation, open-source, automation
  • Core insight: Building self-improving AI agents requires bridging online production tracing with offline evaluation and human-governed feedback loops.

- **Explanation**: If agents completely automate the creation of evaluation datasets and fixes without human oversight, they risk overfitting to quirks and introducing jargon leakage.
- **Evidence**: Customer support agents leaking internal pipeline jargon to end users.
- **Practical implication**: Maintain human-in-the-loop review for dataset boundaries and evaluation criteria.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### The Continuous OSS Agent Improvement Loop
- **How it works**: Production traces and user feedback are captured online, fed into offline evaluation datasets, tested against new candidate prompts or agent configurations, and redeployed after verification.
- **Components**:
  - Roadmap / Meta loop
  - Goal loop
  - Agent turn / Token loop
  - Trace & Monitoring
  - Dataset curation
  - Offline Evaluation
- **When to use**: When developing production-grade AI agents that need to adapt and improve based on real-world usage.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A changelog writer agent analyzes merged PRs, drafts changelog updates, and submits them for human or automated code review.
- **Illustrates**: How an agent stack can automate developer workflows while maintaining quality through review gates.
- **Lesson**: Agents can handle tedious documentation and changelog generation if backed by robust evaluation criteria and human review.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Implement robust tracing and monitoring for all agent runs.
  - Capture user feedback and failure patterns directly into offline evaluation datasets.
- **Strategic**:
  - Design agent workflows to be read-intensive rather than write-intensive by letting agents analyze traces.
  - Strike the right balance of human-agent collaboration by retaining human control over eval criteria and dataset boundaries.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How can we further automate dataset curation without risking data drift or overfitting?
  - What is the optimal frequency for running agent self-improvement loops in production?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Models have matured enough to automate prompt and agent code fixes based on offline evaluation results. (technical trend)
## Notable Quotes
> "I don't write prompts anymore. I have loops."
## Compressed Summary
- Open-source agent stacks are evolving toward self-improvement via continuous feedback loops.
- Combining online tracing with offline evaluation allows agents to propose prompt and code fixes.
- Human-in-the-loop oversight is essential for setting evaluation criteria and preventing overfitting or jargon leakage.
- **Keywords**: agents, observability, evaluation, open-source, automation
- **Core insight**: Building self-improving AI agents requires bridging online production tracing with offline evaluation and human-governed feedback loops.
